catalog_quote: The placement of stress in Wanano falls, in the great majority of cases, on the final syllable of the root. [...] we can analyze Wanano syllables as organized into either bimoraic feet (the predominate pattern corresponding to root morphemes) or monomoraic feet (weak or deficient feet corresponding primarily to bound inflectional and derivational morphemes). sweep_summary: Kotiria (guan1269) is not in the catalog. The only stress/accent/prosody-titled bibliography item is Stenzel 2007 IJAL 73(3) 'Glottalization and Other Suprasegmental Features in Wanano' (doi:10.1086/521730). It is relevant (root-level tone/accent of this language, primarily glottalization) but only its abstract was obtainable: the publisher PDF returns 403, JSTOR requires login, the Icesi repository record that OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar list as open access is a bare redirect to the DOI, Unpaywall shows no OA copy, and fatcat/IA Scholar were rate-limited. The abstract says roots are lexically marked for nasalization and tone but makes no placement statement. The open Portuguese precursor (Stenzel 2005 ABRALIN, on file) gives the same analysis: four contrastive root melodies BAB/BA/AB/A and an H tone ('acento') normally on the second mora of the bimoraic root. Best first-hand statement read: Stenzel 2004 dissertation sec. 2.3.3.2 pp. 76-77 (already on file) — stress falls on the final syllable of the (bimoraic, right-headed) root, which is the leftmost and prominent foot of the phonological word; H tone co-occurs with this stress; system provisionally described as tonal.; updated). Acquisition priority for the 2007 full text: medium (would refine the tone-melody analysis; the placement statement is already covered by Stenzel 2004/2005; Stenzel 2013 UNL grammar remains the likely best printed statement, not obtainable here).

[...] we can analyze Wanano syllables as organized into either bimoraic feet (the predominate pattern corresponding to root morphemes) or monomoraic feet (weak or deficient feet corresponding primarily to bound inflectional and derivational morphemes). [...] at the level of the phonological word, the parameter for prominence is set to the left. The result is that in a fully composed phonological word, it is the leftmost foot which is prominent. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (452-page author-supplied PDF from Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendaju, text layer). At sec. 2.3.3.2 'Foot parameters', printed p.76 (txt lines 4240-4279) every quoted sentence is present word for word; the [...] marks only skip intervening sentences ('So far, we have examined syllable shapes...', the Ewen & van der Hulst citation, the '(prominence is marked +)' parenthesis and the foot diagram). Surrounding section read: 2.3.3.1 (pp.73-75) says weight is not a product of rhyme shape (no codas; devoiced (C)V syllables never stressed), every nucleus = one mora, roots overwhelmingly bimoraic, c. 60 monosyllabic roots from initial-syllable loss show compensatory lengthening (fn.29 cites Wa…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and root-bound: roots (word-initial, mostly bimoraic CV.CV / CV.V) form a right-headed foot and the word gives prominence to its leftmost foot, so primary stress falls on the final (second) syllable/mora of the root, i.e. normally the second syllable of the word; suffixes are unstressed. Pitch is analysed separately as lexical tone (root melodies (<L>)H and (<L>)HL spreading rightward through the phonological word), with the first H tone falling in the root and co-occurring with stress (p. 92); Stenzel notes the system matches Hyman's pitch-accent prototype but provisionally labels it tonal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; Stenzel reports Waltz's view that H tones of any 'secondary accents' within a phonological word are lowered, one H peak per phonological word (p. 83).
new_statements.exceptions: 'in the great majority of cases' — monosyllabic roots that lost an initial syllable (ko 'water', ~ta 'rock', c. 60 roots per Waltz 2002) surface lengthened CV: and carry the stress; devoiced (C)V̥ syllables are never stressed; tonal melody AB/H roots (H on first mora) exist per Stenzel 2005 fn. 6, implying some root-initial H.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (root + suffixes; in compounds the leftmost head root governs); stress and H tone coincide on the root; statement concerns word-level forms, not phrase-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Wanano = Guanano = Kotiria (self-designation), same language guan1269 / ISO gvc; Stenzel's data are from Kotiria communities on the upper Vaupés (Brazil/Colombia border), Waltz & Waltz's from Colombian villages (Villa Fátima, Santa Cruz). No dialect split relevant to the stress statement is reported.

new_statements.citation: Stenzel, Kristine Sue. 2004. A Reference Grammar of Wanano. PhD dissertation, University of Colorado at Boulder.
new_statements.reading: Stress is fixed on the final (second) mora/syllable of the bimoraic root; the root is always the leftmost foot of the phonological word and is the word's prominent foot, so word stress = root-final syllable (word-initial bimoraic foot, right-headed). Stenzel treats this stress as co-occurring with the first H tone of the root's lexical tonal melody (p. 83, citing Waltz & Waltz 2000:455: 'Primary accent, associated with H tone is predictably located (for the majority of words) on the final syllable of verbal, nominal and adjectival roots') and provisionally calls the overall system tonal rather than pitch-accent (sec. 2.5.2, p. 84). Already on file and already the deciding source in this directory's; this sweep re-read it and found nothing newer that is openly readable.

sources.note: Footnote 6: Wanano suprasegmental tone has four contrastive melodies BAB, BA, AB, A (L H L, L H, H L, H), aligned to left edge of root, one tone per mora; body text: ET roots are bimoraic with 'a associação de um tom A (ou ‘acento’) a uma dessas moras, normalmente a segunda'. No separate stress rule.
